title: Natural Identifiers for Privacy and Data Audits in Large Language Models
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: A post-hoc audit extracts natural random identifiers, generates same-distribution decoys, and ranks them against a trained model to measure privacy without retraining.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, numbered circles 0-4 marking steps, shaded stage labels below
description: A three-panel left-to-right pipeline in rounded black boxes, with gray stage captions underneath. Panel 1, '(ε,δ)-DP training', shows a training-data database icon, a flame arrow labeled (ε,δ)-DP, and a blue LLM box with the OpenAI logo. Panel 2, 'NIDs extraction & GIDs generation', shows a suspect-set database feeding a green-shaded strip of Natural Identifiers (triangle, pentagon, diamond and circle shapes). A downward arrow leads to stacked orange-shaded cards of Generated Identifiers, drawn as hatched copies of the same shapes. Panel 3, 'Post-hoc privacy auditing with NIDs', shows candidate sets V1 to Vm in green, one row per shape type. A judge icon labeled Auditor and the DP LLM sit in blue boxes, and an arrow leads to ranked top-r_i lists. Black numbered circles 0 to 4 mark the steps. The eye goes first to the colorful shape rows and the numbered arrows.
caption: Post-hoc DP auditing with NIDs and their corresponding GIDs. 0 We consider the NIDs as the input to a training procedure M (also referred to as the mechanism), which may satisfy (ε, δ)-DP. 1 Given a suspect dataset, we identify the NIDs. 2 We generate the new c −1 GIDs for each NID. 3 We form the candidate sets V1, · · · , Vm by combining the NIDs with corresponding GIDs. 4 Given the resulting trained model and filtered NIDs with corresponding GIDs, an auditor seeks to infer, for each set Vi, which sample was the NID. To do so, the auditor ranks the samples in Vi from the most to the least likely NID-candidate. A prediction is considered correct if the true NID appears among the top-ri ranked samples, where ri is a predefined threshold.
abstract: Assessing the privacy of large language models (LLMs) presents significant challenges. In particular, most existing methods for auditing differential privacy require the insertion of specially crafted canary data during training, making them impractical for auditing already-trained models without costly retraining. Additionally, dataset inference, which audits whether a suspect dataset was used to train a model, is infeasible without access to a private non-member held-out dataset. Yet, such held-out datasets are often unavailable or difficult to construct for real-world cases since they have to be from the same distribution (IID) as the suspect data. These limitations severely hinder the ability to conduct scalable, post-hoc audits. To enable such audits, this work introduces natural identifiers (NIDs) as a novel solution to the above-mentioned challenges. NIDs are structured random strings, such as cryptographic hashes and shortened URLs, naturally occurring in common LLM training datasets. Their format enables the generation of unlimited additional random strings from the same distribution, which can act as alternative canaries for audits and as same-distribution held-out data for dataset inference. Our evaluation highlights that indeed, using NIDs, we can facilitate post-hoc differential privacy auditing without any retraining and enable dataset inference for any suspect dataset containing NIDs without the need for a private non-member held-out dataset.
